A heater converts electrical power, measured in watts, into heat in such a way that the heat produced is given by the function $h(x)=\left(f(x)\right)^2$.

The heater is plugged into a faulty socket which outputs $x=g(t)$ watts at time $t$ seconds.

In D, $x=1$ repeats and $y=3$ repeats: many to many.

$g(f(x))=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{x}-1}$: domain $x>0,\ x\ne1$.

The domain that works for both is $x>1$ and the range that works for both is $y>0$.

Period $=\dfrac{17\pi}{12}-\dfrac{5\pi}{12}=\pi$, so $a=2$.

Testing option D: $x=-3\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$, $v=6\sin\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$.

$v=0$: $2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}=0,\pi,2\pi,3\pi,\ldots$, so $t=\dfrac{5\pi}{12},\dfrac{11\pi}{12},\dfrac{17\pi}{12},\ldots$ (taking the positive values).

$a=12\cos\left(2t+\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right)$; when $t=0$, $a=12\cos30^\circ=12\times\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}=6\sqrt3$.

$\sin\theta=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ gives $\theta=45^\circ,135^\circ$.

Check solutions: $45^\circ$ and $135^\circ$ do not work in the original equation because $\tan90^\circ$ and $\tan270^\circ$ are undefined. Only $15^\circ$ and $105^\circ$ work: 2 solutions.

$A=\tfrac12(\text{cylinder})+\text{rectangles}=\tfrac12\left[2\pi r^2+2\pi rh\right]+2rh=\pi r^2+\pi rh+2rh$

$=\pi r^2+\pi r\times\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}+2r\times\dfrac{2V}{\pi r^2}=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{r}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r}$

$=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left[\dfrac{\pi}{r}+\dfrac{2}{r}\right]=\pi r^2+\dfrac{2V}{\pi}\left(\dfrac{2+\pi}{r}\right)$

$A=\pi r^2+2Vr^{-1}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-1}$

$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=2\pi r-2Vr^{-2}-\dfrac{4V}{\pi}r^{-2}=0$ for stationary points.

$2\pi r=\dfrac{2V}{r^2}+\dfrac{4V}{\pi r^2}$; multiply through by $\pi r^2$: $2\pi^2r^3=2\pi V+4V$

$r^3=\dfrac{2\pi V+4V}{2\pi^2}=\dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}$, so $r=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{V(\pi+2)}{\pi^2}}$

Check type: $\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=2\pi+4Vr^{-3}+\dfrac{8V}{\pi}r^{-3}>0$ for all $r>0$, i.e. always concave up, so the stationary point must be a local minimum. It is the only stationary point in the domain, so it is the absolute minimum.

Translate right by 4: $y=(x-4+1)^2=(x-3)^2$

Horizontal dilation by $\tfrac43$: $y=\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2$

Vertical dilation by $\tfrac13$: $y=\dfrac13\left(\dfrac{3x}{4}-3\right)^2=\dfrac13\times\dfrac{9}{16}(x-4)^2=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2$

Translate down by 3: $y=\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2-3$

Reflect in the $x$-axis: $y=-\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2+3$

Vertex $(4,3)$.

$y$-intercept: when $x=0$, $y=0$, so $(0,0)$.

$x$-intercepts: when $y=0$, $\dfrac{3}{16}(x-4)^2=3$, $(x-4)^2=16$, $x-4=\pm4$, $x=0$ or $x=8$: $(0,0)$ and $(8,0)$.

Alternatively $y=kx(x-8)$ with $(4,3)$: $3=-16k$, $k=-\dfrac{3}{16}$, i.e. $y=-\dfrac{3}{16}x(x-8)$.

Maximum velocity (positive) must be between $t=1$ and $t=3$.

$v=\dfrac{4t}{t^2+3}-1$

$a=\dfrac{4(t^2+3)-8t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}=\dfrac{12-4t^2}{(t^2+3)^2}=0$ for stationary points.

$4t^2=12$, $t=\sqrt3$ (for $1<t<3$)

$\max v=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{3+3}-1=\dfrac{4\sqrt3}{6}-1=\dfrac{2\sqrt3}{3}-1$ m/s ($\doteq0.1547$ m/s)

$u=3x$, $\dfrac{du}{dx}=3$; $v=\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^3$, $\dfrac{dv}{dx}=-\dfrac34\left(1-\dfrac{x}{4}\right)^2$

$f'(x)=v\dfrac{du}{dx}+u\dfrac{dv}{dx}=3\left(1-\dfrac x4\right)^3-\dfrac{9x}{4}\left(1-\dfrac x4\right)^2=3\left(1-\dfrac x4\right)^2\left[\left(1-\dfrac x4\right)-\dfrac{3x}{4}\right]=3\left(1-\dfrac x4\right)^2(1-x)$

$f'(x)=0$ for stationary points: $x=1$ or $x=4$.

$x=1$: $y=2\dfrac{17}{64}$; $x=4$: $y=1$.

Stationary points at $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$ and $(4,1)$.

Check types: $f'(0)=3$, $f'(1)=0$, $f'(2)=-\dfrac34$, so a local maximum at $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$.

$f'$ is negative on both sides of $x=4$ and $f'(4)=0$, so a horizontal point of inflexion at $(4,1)$.

$f(5)=\dfrac{49}{64}>0$

$f(6)=-\dfrac54<0$

The graph is continuous, so there must be at least one $x$-intercept between $x=5$ and $x=6$.
End points: $(0,1)$ and $\left(6,-1\dfrac14\right)$. Local maximum $\left(1,2\dfrac{17}{64}\right)$, horizontal point of inflexion $(4,1)$, $x$-intercept between $x=5$ and $x=6$.

The first integral $=\dfrac13k=\dfrac13\times\dfrac34=\dfrac14=0.25$.

We want to cover $0.88$, so we still need $0.88-0.25=0.63$.

Call the time $x$: $\dfrac34\displaystyle\int_2^x\left(2-\tfrac t2\right)dt=0.63$

$\left[2t-\dfrac{t^2}{4}\right]_2^x=0.84$

$\left(2x-\dfrac{x^2}{4}\right)-(4-1)=0.84$

$0=\dfrac14x^2-2x+3.84$

$x^2-8x=-15.36$, $(x-4)^2=0.64$, $x-4=\pm0.8$

$x=3.2$ or $4.8$ (not in domain)

Time taken is 3.2 minutes, i.e. 3 min 12 s.

$h(x)=[f(x)]^2$, so $\dfrac{dh}{dx}=2f'(x)f(x)$.

$x=g(t)$, so $\dfrac{dx}{dt}=g'(t)$.

Given: $g(1)=3$ (when $t=1$, $x=3$), $g'(1)=4$, $f(3)=5$, $f'(3)=2$.

$\dfrac{dh}{dt}=\dfrac{dh}{dx}\times\dfrac{dx}{dt}$ (chain rule) $=2f'(x)f(x)g'(t)$

Sub $t=1$, so $x=3$: $\dfrac{dh}{dt}=2f'(3)f(3)g'(1)=2\times2\times5\times4=80$
